courseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops source appraisal, academic argument and presentation.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Economics
courseEvidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
courseEvidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling
courseEvidence.contribution: introduces markets, distribution and macroeconomic relationships needed to analyse the evidenced capitalism and globalisation direction

courseEvidence.name: International Macroeconomics
courseEvidence.description2: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines short-, medium- and long-run macroeconomic dynamics and policy, including international dimensions. Students study goods, financial and labour markets, inflation and unemployment, economic growth, expectations and the open economy. IS-LM and IS-LM-PC models connect markets and policy effects. Algebraic and graphical analysis and interpretation of macroeconomic indicators support the evaluation of economic developments and fiscal and monetary policy.
courseEvidence.topics: Goods and financial markets; Labour markets; Phillips curve; IS-LM and IS-LM-PC models; Economic growth; Saving and capital accumulation; Technological progress; Expectations; Open-economy macroeconomics; Fiscal and monetary policy; Business cycles and economic crises
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical macroeconomic analysis; IS-LM and IS-LM-PC modelling; Macroeconomic data and indicator analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: studies business cycles, goods and financial markets and policy effects as explanations of modern economic change

courseEvidence.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courseEvidence.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
courseEvidence.topics: Choice under uncertainty; Non-egoistic preferences; Cognitive limitations; Monopoly; Imperfect competition and strategic behaviour; Labour markets; Capital markets; General equilibrium; Market efficiency; Externalities; Government intervention
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses incentives, strategic interaction and equilibrium as the economic mechanisms underlying the evidenced capitalism and inequality questions

courseEvidence.name: Public Economics
courseEvidence.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
courseEvidence.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
courseEvidence.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research
courseEvidence.contribution: studies market failure, taxation, redistribution and public spending as explicit mechanisms of inequality and government economic power

courseEvidence.name: Econometrics
courseEvidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courseEvidence.contribution: provides OLS/GLS/IV inference, tests and a Stata empirical paper as economic analysis; a historical dataset or historical-research application is not guaranteed

courseEvidence.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courseEvidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
courseEvidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: provides general research design and statistics to complement historical enquiry; it does not teach the specialised historical-source work of History by Numbers

courseEvidence.name: Modern History
courseEvidence.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
courseEvidence.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
courseEvidence.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development
courseEvidence.contribution: surveys industrialisation, revolutions, world wars, decolonisation and European integration from 1815 to 2025

courseEvidence.name: Histories of Gender
courseEvidence.description2: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
courseEvidence.topics: Gender and intersectionality; Body sovereignty; Heteronormativity and compulsory heterosexuality; Homonationalism; Rainbow capitalism; Masculinity and sexuality; Queer ageing and memory; Slavery and racialized gender histories; Family and socialization; Health and pathologization; Media bias and book bans; Incarceration; Queer activism and resistance
courseEvidence.methods: Historical primary-source research; Intersectional analysis; Oral-history interviewing; Critical interpretation of memoir and cultural representations; Arts-based research; Community-engaged activist art; Reflective analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: investigates nineteenth- to twenty-first-century gender histories using storytelling, interviews and historical interpretation

courseEvidence.name: History of Empires
courseEvidence.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
courseEvidence.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development
courseEvidence.contribution: examines the rise and fall of world empires, their historical sources of power and competing historical explanations

courseEvidence.name: Ways of War
courseEvidence.description2: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys Western warfare from antiquity to the present and examines the contested claim that a distinctive military trajectory helped produce Western global dominance. Weapons, technology, strategy, tactics, institutions and soldiers' experience are studied across land, sea and air warfare. Research analyzes a strategic text, a commander's performance or a battle from the individual soldier's perspective, using primary sources and historical scholarship.
courseEvidence.topics: Western warfare and global power; Ancient infantry and Roman warfare; Medieval warfare; Gunpowder and naval warfare; Overseas conquest; Dynastic and national warfare; Industrialization of war; World wars; Cold War and nuclear strategy; Guerrilla warfare and terrorism; Military leadership; Soldiers' experience, morale and cohesion; Future warfare
courseEvidence.methods: Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historiographical critique of strategic texts; Historical analysis of military command; Soldier-centered battle analysis; Analysis of diaries, memoirs and combat accounts
courseEvidence.contribution: studies warfare from antiquity to the present and critically examines its proposed role in Western global hegemony

courseEvidence.name: Native American Histories
courseEvidence.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
courseEvidence.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
courseEvidence.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production
courseEvidence.contribution: studies Native American social and cultural histories, colonial forced schooling, migration and cultural resistance through Indigenous methodologies

courseEvidence.name: Researching the “American Century”
courseEvidence.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops historical questions, critical work with sources and a substantial research paper in American history.

courseEvidence.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
courseEvidence.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
courseEvidence.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: traces rights from early-modern natural law to constitutional declarations and twentieth-century expansion, connecting political violence with legal and philosophical responses

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
courseEvidence.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
courseEvidence.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development
courseEvidence.contribution: introduces central Western philosophical arguments from antiquity onward as intellectual context; the specific VU Key Texts reading list is not established and no course equivalence is claimed

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
courseEvidence.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
courseEvidence.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction
courseEvidence.contribution: compares historical theories of state authority from classical antiquity to the present and their relation to contemporary political problems

courseEvidence.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
courseEvidence.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
courseEvidence.topics: Democracy and authoritarianism; Democratization and democratic backsliding; States, nations and nationalism; Constitutions and courts; Executives, legislatures and bureaucracies; Political economy; Parties and party systems; Populism and technocracy; Elections and electoral systems; Political culture and polarization; Political participation; Interest groups and public policy
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation
courseEvidence.contribution: examines development and breakdown of democratic and authoritarian regimes, state institutions and globalisation as the political dimension of historical change

courseEvidence.name: Theory of International Relations
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
courseEvidence.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting
courseEvidence.contribution: applies international-relations theories to historical and contemporary geopolitical cases relevant to empire, war and migration

courseEvidence.name: European Union Politics
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
courseEvidence.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
courseEvidence.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies European integration and policy institutions and uses European Parliament amendments for empirical institutional research.

courseEvidence.name: Peace & Conflict
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
courseEvidence.topics: Conflict theories and structural violence; Identity and historical grievances; Colonialism and forced migration; International peace and security; Humanitarian law and human rights; Positive, negative and hybrid peace; Local peacebuilding; Frozen conflicts; Counterterrorism and rule of law; Transitional justice; Gender and conflict; Development and peacebuilding; Reconciliation, arts and religion; Global South perspectives; Travelling concepts and researcher positionality
courseEvidence.methods: Interdisciplinary Research Process; Cross-disciplinary travelling-concept analysis; Conflict case analysis; Context and stakeholder mapping; Annotated bibliography and evidence synthesis; Policy-option appraisal; Policy-brief and background-dossier development; Researcher positionality analysis; Comparative research podcast production
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses past and present violence, colonial grievances, truth and reconciliation through historically grounded conflict and peacebuilding theories

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Sociology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
courseEvidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation
courseEvidence.contribution: studies classical social theories in their historical imperial and colonial settings and interrogates the treatment of race and gender

courseEvidence.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courseEvidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
courseEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: practises qualitative interviewing and interpretation of situated social processes, complementing historical oral-source and research training

courseEvidence.name: Modern Sociology
courseEvidence.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
courseEvidence.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
courseEvidence.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research
courseEvidence.contribution: studies theories of modernity through the history of imperialism and colonial responses, implementing the evidenced European global-legacy direction

courseEvidence.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
courseEvidence.contribution: investigates environmental-justice movements and anti-colonial struggles through specific case studies, implementing the evidenced global environmental strand

courseEvidence.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courseEvidence.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
courseEvidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
courseEvidence.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design
courseEvidence.contribution: uses civil-society theories, migrant solidarity and community-engaged organisation study for contemporary social-inclusion application; it does not form a migration-history sequence or guarantee a future partner

courseEvidence.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courseEvidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
courseEvidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
courseEvidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting
courseEvidence.contribution: provides regression, factor analysis and multivariate inference as transferable tools; historical numerical-source selection and visualisation remain a separate gap

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Western Art History
courseEvidence.description2: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
courseEvidence.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
courseEvidence.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: interprets Western art from the Renaissance onward as historical evidence shaped by institutions, markets and historiography

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
courseEvidence.description2: Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
courseEvidence.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
courseEvidence.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development
courseEvidence.contribution: studies artefact production and social, gendered and religious identities across ancient settlements and world regions, using archaeological evidence

courseEvidence.name: African Art & Heritage
courseEvidence.description2: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.
courseEvidence.topics: Western African artistic traditions; Sculpture, masks and visual languages; Art, religion and social authority; Regional traditions in Nigeria, the Niger region, Atlantic forests and Congo; African influences on European modernism; Harlem Renaissance and diaspora; Art Nègre and the Ecole de Dakar; Colonial looting; Universal museums; Museum acquisition and display; Restitution and repatriation
courseEvidence.methods: Visual and contextual art-historical analysis; Comparative interpretation of artistic traditions; Analysis of primary artistic and critical texts; Heritage-restitution case analysis; Scholarly literature review and annotated bibliography; Independent art-historical research
courseEvidence.contribution: examines African religious and cultural visual traditions, colonial collecting and contested repatriation of heritage

courseEvidence.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
courseEvidence.description2: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies Renaissance Italian art and its cross-cultural connections through Mediterranean exchange.

courseEvidence.name: Greek Archaeology
courseEvidence.description2: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.
courseEvidence.contribution: investigates community and democracy in early-democratic Greece through archaeological evidence

courseEvidence.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
courseEvidence.description2: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
courseEvidence.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
courseEvidence.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research
courseEvidence.contribution: studies curatorial practice and the historical institutions that shape public memory and the interpretation of modern art

courseEvidence.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
courseEvidence.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
courseEvidence.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
courseEvidence.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design
courseEvidence.contribution: investigates Athenian democracy, exclusion, myth, religion and its archaeological heritage, using ancient sources and an assembly simulation

courseEvidence.name: Writing Art's Histories
courseEvidence.description2: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
courseEvidence.contribution: Traces art-historical methods from the sixteenth century through critical readings of disciplinary scholarship.

courseEvidence.name: World Myth & Literature
courseEvidence.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
courseEvidence.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
courseEvidence.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation
courseEvidence.contribution: Compares myths across cultures and studies their reception, narrative agency and use in cultural expression.

courseEvidence.name: Life & Travel Writing
courseEvidence.description2: Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.
courseEvidence.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity
courseEvidence.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing
courseEvidence.contribution: critically interprets memoirs, diaries, autobiographies and travel narratives as situated life stories relevant to historical source criticism

courseEvidence.name: Media Archaeology
courseEvidence.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
courseEvidence.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
courseEvidence.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses obsolete media and early books as material historical evidence of communication, knowledge circulation and memory

courseEvidence.name: Media & the Environment
courseEvidence.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
courseEvidence.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse
courseEvidence.methods: Close film, image and sound analysis; Comparative analysis of media forms and representational strategies; Ecocritical interpretation; Theory-based analytical or creative media inquiry
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses Anthropocene, deep-time, Indigenous and postcolonial environmental narratives as cultural evidence of changing human-environment relations

courseEvidence.name: Media & Race
courseEvidence.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
courseEvidence.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
courseEvidence.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection
courseEvidence.contribution: researches nineteenth- to twenty-first-century racial oppression and resistance through American media and historical cultural expression

courseEvidence.name: The Documentary
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
courseEvidence.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
courseEvidence.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice
courseEvidence.contribution: traces documentary history and evaluates non-fiction representations within their historical, ethical and social contexts

comparability: Each option retains the six-course historical core, including modern history, gender and interviews, empire, warfare, Indigenous histories and a sustained research paper on American history. The first option builds cultural and public-memory interpretation through art, archaeology, narrative and media. The second develops political institutions, rights, conflict and social inclusion. The third builds economic explanation and inference alongside institutional and social inquiry. No separate crime or migration-history sequence is supported. VU retains period and regional depth and specialist historical methods beyond these UCR options.
repair: In the heritage option, Histories of Gender moves earlier and World Myth & Literature replaces Great Literary Works. Both contribute narrative interpretation, while the new course adds cross-cultural transmission and reception. In the political economy option, European Union Politics replaces Media & the Environment, adding integration, governance and empirical analysis. Introduction to Economics moves into the first term, with Histories of Gender also moved earlier and introductory Sociology moved to year two. No set of term moves alone fits the alternating offering pattern in either affected option. The conflict option retains all courses and terms. The three options preserve six History courses and the final American-history seminar.
alignments: Both examine modern European change. UCR begins in the nineteenth century and also follows developments beyond Europe.
Both use interviews to investigate the past. UCR applies them to North American gender histories, while VU also teaches preparation of interviews for digital archives.
Both examine historical changes across world regions. UCR focuses on empires, and VU surveys world history more broadly.
Both develop historical research questions and use sources to build an argument. UCR’s seminar focuses on American history, while VU’s seminar studies early modern knowledge in the Netherlands.
UCR studies ancient societies through material evidence. VU follows the changing Mediterranean world across a much longer period.
Both address early modern European culture. UCR focuses on Renaissance Italian art and exchange, while VU covers a wider period and range of historical changes.

VU requires a 9 EC individual thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

VU develops specialist methods for interpreting photography and photographic archives in political history.
